title: Senior's toolkit: passwords and login in .NET
summary: The framework APIs for hashing and checking passwords, random secrets, constant-time comparison and rate-limiting the login endpoint.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: passwords and login in .NET
steps.body: You built password hashing by hand to understand it. At work you use the framework pieces that already get the details right. These are the ones experienced .NET developers reach for.

toolkit.what: ASP.NET Core Identity's hasher (PBKDF2 with a random salt, versioned format). Use it even without the rest of Identity. Package: `Microsoft.Extensions.Identity.Core`.
flags: returns a self-describing string to store
correct password but old settings: hash again and save

toolkit.what: One-call PBKDF2 when you control the format yourself. Use the static method; the old `Rfc2898DeriveBytes` constructors are obsolete.
flags: never the SHA-1 default of older code

toolkit.what: Cryptographically secure random bytes for salts, reset tokens and session ids. `Random` is predictable and must never be used for secrets.
flags: a random hex string of 32 characters
random text from your own alphabet
toolkit.example:
byte[] salt = RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(16);
string resetToken = RandomNumberGenerator.GetHexString(64);

toolkit.what: Compare secrets (hashes, tokens, API keys) in time that does not depend on where they differ, so an attacker cannot learn them byte by byte.
flags: compare bytes; hash or decode strings first
returns false at once (length is not secret)

toolkit.what: Slow down password guessing at the endpoint. Built into ASP.NET Core; combine with lockout per account.
flags: the default is 503, which looks like an outage
the middleware must be in the pipeline

steps.prompt: Match each result of `VerifyHashedPassword` to what you do.
pairs: sign in, then hash again with current settings and save
reject with the same message as an unknown user

steps.prompt: A penetration test reports that password reset links can be guessed: two links issued a second apart share most of their characters. Which line is the cause?
steps.explain: `Random` is fast and predictable, and a 32-bit value is far too short anyway. Anything an attacker must not guess comes from `RandomNumberGenerator`, with at least 128 bits.

steps.prompt: Hash a new password with PBKDF2 and a fresh salt.
You added a rate limit to `/login`. Under a guessing attack, monitoring pages the on-call engineer: "login returning 503 Service Unavailable". What is wrong?
options: The limiter is working, but it rejects with 503 by default; set `RejectionStatusCode = 429` so clients and alerts see Too Many Requests
Fixed-window limiters always return 503 and cannot be changed
steps.explain: 503 says the server is broken; 429 says the client is going too fast. The right code keeps alerts quiet, tells well-behaved clients to back off, and is what API gateways expect.

items: `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals` to check an API key hash
`new Rfc2898DeriveBytes(password, salt)` with its default settings
steps.explain: A plain SHA-256 is far too fast to slow down guessing. `==` stops at the first different character. The old constructor defaults to SHA-1 and 1,000 iterations.

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: When you see auth code in review, check three things: passwords go through a slow, salted hasher; every secret comes from `RandomNumberGenerator`; every secret comparison is fixed-time. Put a rate limit returning 429 on login, reset and any endpoint that checks a code.
